title: The Role of an ISA
summary: What an Instruction Set Architecture actually defines, and why it's the stable contract compilers and hardware both target.

slides.subTitle: Hardware meets software here
slides.markdown:
An **Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)** is the agreed vocabulary between software and hardware — the exact set of instructions, registers, and memory rules a CPU promises to support. A compiler targets the ISA, not the physical chip.

Think of it like a restaurant menu: the kitchen (hardware) can change staff, equipment, and technique freely, but as long as it keeps serving what's on the menu (the ISA), every customer's order (compiled program) still works. Change the menu, and every order written against it breaks.

This is why a 2010 x86 binary still runs on a 2026 x86 chip: the **contract never moved**, even though everything under it did.

slides.subTitle: What varies below the line
slides.markdown:
Below the ISA sits the **microarchitecture** — the actual implementation: how many pipeline stages, how big the caches are, whether execution is in-order or out-of-order. None of that is visible to software.

Intel and AMD both implement the x86-64 ISA, but their internal pipelines are entirely different designs. A program can't tell which chip it's running on just by its instruction encoding — only by timing.

This separation is deliberate: it lets hardware teams **redesign the engine every few years** while every existing binary, compiler, and OS keeps working unmodified.

slides.subTitle: One interface, many implementations
slides.markdown:
The distinction interviewers probe most: **what's fixed** vs **what's free to change**.

| | ISA | Microarchitecture |
|---|---|---|
| Defines | Instructions, registers, memory model | Pipeline, cache sizes, execution order |
| Visible to | Compilers, assembly programmers | Chip designers only |
| Changes | Rarely, with strict backward compatibility | Every new chip generation |
| Example | x86-64, ARMv8, RISC-V | Skylake vs Zen vs Cortex-X4 |

To decide which bucket something falls in, ask: **can software detect it directly?** If yes, it's ISA; if only timing reveals it, it's microarchitecture.

An ISA is a full spec, not just a list of opcodes. It nails down:

- **Instructions** — the operations available and how they're encoded.
- **Registers** — how many, how wide, and their special roles (PC, stack pointer).
- **Memory model** — addressable unit size, byte ordering, alignment rules.
- **Calling convention** — often standardized alongside it, though technically an ABI concern.

Miss any one of these and a compiler can't reliably generate code — it needs every detail pinned down, because it never sees the chip it's compiling for.

slides.subTitle: From C to gates
slides.markdown:
The ISA is one layer in a much taller stack, and it's the layer where the **hardware/software boundary** sits.

![Abstraction stack from high-level language down to gates, with the ISA marking the hardware/software boundary](assets/abstraction-stack.svg)

Everything above the ISA line (language, compiler, assembly) is software's problem; everything below (microarchitecture, gates, transistors) is hardware's problem. Compilers translate down to the ISA and stop — they never need to know what's beneath it.

slides.subTitle: "Faster CPU" vs "different ISA"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This new CPU is way faster, so it must have a smarter instruction set."

**Why it's wrong:** Two chips can share the exact same ISA and differ enormously in speed — deeper pipelines, bigger caches, better branch prediction, more execution units. None of that changes a single instruction's encoding.

**Correct model:** ISA generation ≠ performance generation. Apple's M-series and a 2013 ARM chip can both be ARMv8; the speed gap is almost entirely microarchitecture, not the instruction set.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending an ISA without breaking it
slides.subTitle: Feature bits and optional extensions
slides.markdown:
If the ISA is a fixed contract, how do brand-new instructions (like AVX-512's wide vector ops) ever get added? By making them **optional extensions**, detected at runtime rather than assumed. x86 exposes a `CPUID` instruction that reports which extensions a given chip actually supports; RISC-V's whole ISA is built from composable lettered extensions (`M` for multiply, `A` for atomics, `V` for vector) that a chip can mix and match.

Software that wants to use a new instruction must check the feature bit first and fall back to the old encoding if it's absent — skip that check and the binary works on the chip it was tested on and **crashes with an illegal-instruction fault** on any chip lacking the extension. This is exactly how the base ISA contract stays stable release after release while genuinely new capability still ships.

slides.sectionTitle: Endianness is part of the contract too
slides.subTitle: Byte order isn't an implementation detail
slides.markdown:
**Endianness** — whether a multi-byte value's most significant byte is stored first (big-endian) or last (little-endian) — is specified by the ISA, not left to the chip designer's whim, because software that reads raw memory byte-by-byte (network protocol parsing, casting a `char*` over an `int`, cross-machine serialization) needs to know which order to expect.

x86 and RISC-V default little-endian; network protocols conventionally specify big-endian ("network byte order"), which is exactly why socket code calls `htons`/`ntohs` to convert — a raw multi-byte integer read off the wire on a little-endian machine is silently byte-reversed garbage without that conversion, even though every individual byte transferred correctly.

slides.sectionTitle: Not every ISA targets a general-purpose CPU
slides.subTitle: Domain-specific instruction sets
slides.markdown:
Everything so far assumed a general-purpose CPU ISA, but the same contract idea applies to specialized hardware: a GPU's SIMT instruction set is built around thousands of threads executing the same instruction on different data lanes; a DSP's ISA bakes in fused multiply-accumulate as a first-class primitive because signal-processing math lives on it; a TPU's ISA is built almost entirely around matrix-multiply-and-accumulate tiles.

The trade-off is always the same shape: a domain-specific ISA sacrifices general-purpose flexibility for far higher throughput on its one workload class, because every transistor and encoding bit goes toward that workload instead of being spread across a broad, flexible instruction set. Recognizing which category a given chip's ISA falls into — general-purpose vs domain-specific — is what tells you whether "why doesn't this run arbitrary code well" even makes sense as a question to ask.
